title: OpenAI 终止与 Cursor 合作，11 月 12 日生效
content:
We unfortunately have decided that we cannot continue providing access to our models through Cursor and are ending our partnership. It boils down to trust and we’ve asked that this takes effect on November 12 to give you some time to plan.
Many have used the GPT models through Cursor and here are options we know should work in the future:
• We will continue to allow using your own OpenAI API key and similarly will continue to provide access through our IDE extensions for Cursor. • We will keep working with the broadest range of tools and harnesses, some of which are OSS, but also many many closed-source ones.
We are as committed as ever to continue supporting developers and the flourishing ecosystem of tools, harnesses and products. We will also continue to invest in our own open-source initiatives and believe in broad optionality for developers.
You can read more about our decision in the blog: https://openai.com/index/our-decision-on-cursor-following-its-acquisition-by-spacex/

report.summary: OpenAI ends direct Cursor access over trust concerns after SpaceX acquisition, effective Nov 12; developers can still use API keys.
report.background: OpenAI and Cursor, a popular AI-powered code editor, have had a close partnership, with OpenAI models powering many features. The relationship broke down after Cursor was acquired by SpaceX, raising concerns about ownership and alignment. OpenAI says it decided it cannot continue providing its models through Cursor, citing trust. The termination takes effect November 12. To soften the transition, OpenAI will still allow Cursor users to connect their own OpenAI API key and will continue providing IDE extensions for Cursor. OpenAI also stresses ongoing support for a broad range of developer tools, both open-source and closed-source, and says it remains invested in its own open-source efforts. The move reflects growing tension in the AI ecosystem as model providers and application companies navigate acquisitions and control over distribution.
key_points: The partnership ends on November 12. OpenAI tells developers it can no longer provide access to its models through Cursor, framing the decision as a matter of trust. This gives users a short window to make alternative arrangements before the cut-off.

Cursor's acquisition by SpaceX triggered the split. OpenAI's linked blog title explicitly references the acquisition, suggesting the change in ownership created conflicts or concerns about how OpenAI models would be used and governed within a company led by Elon Musk, who is often critical of OpenAI.

Users are not left without options. OpenAI will continue to allow developers to bring their own OpenAI API key to Cursor, and existing IDE extensions for Cursor will keep working. This means many workflows can continue, though users may need to manage billing and keys themselves.

OpenAI reaffirms its commitment to developer choice. The company says it will support the broadest range of tools, including open-source and closed-source projects, and will keep investing in its own open-source initiatives. This is likely intended to reassure developers worried about reduced flexibility.

The move could reshape the AI coding tool market. By pulling direct model access from a major editor, OpenAI is signalling it wants more control over how its models are distributed and monetized, potentially pushing Cursor toward competitors like Anthropic or Google.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this marks a notable shift in power dynamics. Model providers are becoming less willing to let third-party tools act as intermediaries, especially when ownership changes raise strategic or philosophical conflicts. Developers using Cursor will feel the most immediate impact: they'll need to configure their own OpenAI API key or explore alternative models, which could bring extra costs, latency, and management overhead. For regular users, Cursor's built-in AI features may change or switch providers, possibly affecting quality and behaviour. OpenAI benefits by strengthening direct relationships with developers and pushing its own ecosystem, including IDE extensions and open-source tools. The episode is also a warning that integrations between AI companies and their distribution partners can be fragile, so businesses should avoid locking themselves into a single vendor stack.
report.tools: If you want to keep using OpenAI models in Cursor, start with your own OpenAI API key and the official IDE extensions. Also watch OpenAI's open-source Codex CLI, which offers an agentic coding experience. For Cursor alternatives with varied model support, try Continue.dev or Aider; both allow switching between OpenAI, Anthropic, and local models. Cursor itself may soon lean more on non-OpenAI models, so monitor its release notes.
